title: Claude Fable 5.2 for Revit and AutoCAD Drawing Review
summary: Use Claude Fable 5.2 in ArchiLabs Desktop to trace a doorway callout to its detail. See what the drawing benchmark measured and how to review the result.
body_markdown:
Imagine an installer following the detail bubble beside a new vestibule door. The reference takes her to the right sheet and the wrong drawing. Detail 4 shows the sill at a fixed storefront panel. The door threshold she needs is detail 6, a few inches to the right on the very same sheet. A check that merely confirms the sheet exists will pass this mistake every time.


**Claude Fable 5.2 is available in ArchiLabs Desktop for Revit and AutoCAD.** Anthropic released Fable 5.2 on November 9, 2026, with improvements in vision and reasoning. For a drawing reviewer, the interesting question is how far those skills get you from the bubble on the plan to the detail the installer actually needs.[Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 release](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-fable-and-mythos-5-2)


## Claude Fable 5.2 on architectural drawing benchmarks


COXIT tested Fable 5.2 on 119 architectural drawing pages with objects marked by human reviewers. For callouts, Fable located **535 of 557** , missed 22, and marked 49 extra locations. That earned **94% F1** for callouts, a score that accounts for both misses and extra marks. Across all five object categories, its overall F1 was 85%.[COXIT’s CaseVBench results and annotated drawings](https://coxit.co/blog/claude-fable-5-2-architectural-drawings/)


The researchers scored whether each box landed on the right object. On your vestibule sheet, that would mean finding the bubble beside the door. To tell the installer where to look, you still have to read the reference, open the destination, and check what the section cuts through. That gives Fable a specific job in Desktop.


## Use Claude Fable 5.2 for Revit detail review


Bring the entrance plan and the detail sheet from the same issue into ArchiLabs Desktop. Identify the vestibule door in Revit. Give Fable the design question as well as the sheet numbers, so it has a reason to look beyond a matching digit.


> Follow the detail reference at this door. Give me the plan sheet, the printed detail and sheet number, and the title of the destination view. Does the section show the door threshold or a fixed panel sill? Point to the feature that tells you.


A threshold section might show the bottom rail of the moving door. The adjacent panel section might show glazing seated in a sill pocket. If the print is too coarse to tell, bring up the larger detail view. Once the architect confirms which view applies, inspect how the reference was made. A Revit reference callout points to a view, and its displayed identifiers follow that view’s sheet placement. For a reference callout, select the bubble and change its referenced view. Open the detail from the plan and follow the same path the installer will take.[Autodesk’s guide to reference callouts](https://help.autodesk.com/cloudhelp/2026/ENU/RevitLT-DocumentPresent/files/GUID-FF015E39-0B0B-49C3-9AA1-F0AA0303716C.htm)


## Claude Fable 5.2 for AutoCAD sheet references


In a DWG set, that bubble might be an attributed block with separately entered detail and sheet numbers. Select the occurrence beside the vestibule door in Desktop. If both details share a sheet, ask Fable to change the detail attribute on that instance from 4 to 6. Other instances of the block may still correctly point to the storefront sill. If the number comes from a Sheet Set field, check which view the field references before changing it.


Plot the entrance plan, open the detail it names, and read both titles together. The person holding the prints now has a route from the door on the plan to the section that explains its threshold. To try this in Desktop, bring one suspect reference, its destination sheet, and the question the drawing needs to answer.[Work with Claude in ArchiLabs Desktop](https://archilabs.ai/desktop)
